title: Named by deeds
hookLine: no one can tell all His names; the wise name Him by His works (Jaap 1)

lines: NEIGHBORS WHOSE NAMES YOU NEVER LEARNED.
THE ONE WHO HOLDS THE ELEVATOR.
cards: Every apartment building has them: neighbors whose names you never learned. So you name them by what they do. The guy who waters the plants at six.
The woman who always holds the elevator. The kid practicing trumpet, badly, with total commitment. You don't know who they are on paper.
You know them by their deeds, and that might be the truer name. The first stanza of Jaap Sahib ends on exactly this idea.

teach.h: NET NET: NOT THIS, NOT THIS.
teach.b: The first stanza has stripped away every label: no mark, no caste, no form anyone can draw. It has called the One king of kings. Now, its last two lines.
First the whole of creation speaks: gods, humans, demons, even the forests and the grass, and what they say is net net. Not this, not this.
It's a very old phrase in Indian thought, for a reality so large that every description has to be refused.

teach.h: WHO CAN TELL ALL YOUR NAMES?
teach.b: Then the question the stanza has been building to: who can tell all Your names? Nobody. And the answer: the wise speak Your karam naam.
Karam means deeds, works, actions. Naam means name. Names drawn from what You do.
That's the hinge of the whole hymn. Everything Jaap is about to say, salutation to the Merciful, to the Protector, the Giver, the Destroyer of cruelty, these are deed-names. Not a passport.
A list of what the One has been seen to do.

Guru Arjan says something close in the Guru Granth Sahib, on page one thousand eighty-three: the tongue speaks names made from Your deeds, and Sat Naam, the true Name, is Your name from before all beginnings.
So Sikhs hold two things together. There's a Name beyond all naming.
And there are countless names that come from noticing: mercy here, protection there, a gift that arrived on time.
The wise, Jaap says, don't argue about the first. They keep a record of the second.

how: Sikhs use many names for the Divine, Waheguru, Akal Purakh, Gobind, Kartar, and many of them, like Kartar (the Creator) and Dayal (the Merciful), are names drawn from what the One does.

o: names for the One drawn from what He does
a name earned by your own good karma
a title the emperors gave to holy men

games.q: named by deeds — tap the pairs.

s: Jaap claims the wise know all of God's names
it asks who can tell all Your names, and answers: the wise speak the names drawn from Your deeds.
in the first stanza even the forests and grass say 'not this, not this'
all creation joins in refusing any final description.
the Guru Granth Sahib has a similar idea about names from deeds
Guru Arjan, Ang 1083: the tongue speaks deed-names; Sat Naam is the primal Name.

games.q: you want to name the One who has no mark and no form. what does the first stanza of Jaap say the wise do?
games.why: karam naam barnat sumat: the wise describe Your deed-names. the rest of Jaap is exactly that, a long list of what the One does.

practice: Name one thing you've seen the Divine do, or, if that language doesn't fit you, one thing life did for you that you didn't arrange: a recovery, a stranger's help, a morning that came after a terrible night.
Give it a deed-name, the way Jaap does, the one who sent help, the one who kept me, and breathe with it. If you pray, you can say it with Waheguru; if not, let it simply be a thank-you.

wordCard.voice: Karam naam. Names drawn from what the One does: no one can tell all the One's names, so the wise name Him by His works.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: kirtam naam, names made from deeds, Guru Arjan's phrase on Ang 1083.

carryVoice: Your line: mercy here, protection there. The names come from noticing. Three hundred thirty-five days, and counting.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1083 (Guru Arjan, Maru Solhe): kirtam naam and Sat Naam
